name: Getting Ready to Count — Big, Small, First, Last
whatIsIt: Before we count with numbers, we learn to SORT and COMPARE things: which is bigger or smaller, taller or shorter, which comes FIRST and which comes LAST, and where things are — on top, below, inside, next to. These 'pre-number' ideas are the ground that counting stands on.
whyNeeded: A child who can sort a pile of buttons, line things up, and say 'the big one', 'the first one', or 'the one on top' is ready to count with meaning. Without these ideas, numbers are just sounds. Pre-number sense turns counting into understanding.
realLifeUses: Lining up shoes from smallest to biggest
Knowing who is FIRST and who is LAST in a queue
Putting toys INSIDE the box and the lid ON TOP
Sorting fruit into groups: all the mangoes together, all the bananas together

vocabulary.meaning: Comparing size — which takes up more or less space.
The one at the start of a line, and the one at the end.
Where something is: on, under, inside, next to, top, bottom.
To put things that are alike into the same group.

story.title: First in Line at the Village Fair
story.text: At the village fair, Anu lines up her three new toys on Dadi's shawl: a little wooden car, then a ball, then a cloth doll. 'Which one is FIRST, Anu?' asks Dadi. Anu points to the very start of the line. 'The car is first — it stands right at the beginning. The doll is LAST, at the far end.' Dadi claps. 'Big, small, first, last — you're getting ready to count!'
story.extractedProblem: Three toys stand in a line: a car, a ball, a doll. Which toy is FIRST?
story.answerInStory: The car is first — it stands at the start of the line.

visual.caption: Compare and sort: a small group and a big group. Which is bigger? Getting ready to count!

standardMethod.summary: Compare by looking (size, height), find first and last by the ends of a line, and sort by putting alike things together.
steps: To compare SIZE: look at which takes more space — that is bigger.
To find FIRST and LAST: look at the two ends of the line.
For POSITION: say where it is — on, under, inside, next to.
To SORT: put things that are the same kind into one group.

alternateMethods.name: Line-them-up
alternateMethods.whenToUse: To compare sizes or find order.
steps: Stand the things in a row.
Look from one end: the start is first, the far end is last.
For size, line up bottoms and see which reaches highest.
alternateMethods.example: Three pencils lined up: the longest reaches highest — it is the biggest.

workedExamples.problem: A big elephant and a small ant. Which one is BIGGER?
steps: Look at the space each takes.
The elephant is huge; the ant is tiny.

workedExamples.problem: In a line: cat, dog, cow. Which animal is LAST?
steps: Find the two ends of the line.
Last is at the far end.

visual.caption: cat is FIRST, cow is LAST.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the last one 'first' — mixing up the two ends.
commonMistakes.fix: FIRST is at the START of the line (where you begin). LAST is at the very END. Point to where you'd start reading — that's first.
BIG takes up MORE space; SMALL takes up less. Put them side by side — the one that looks larger is big.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting a banana in the 'apples' group when sorting fruit.
commonMistakes.fix: Sort by ONE feature at a time (kind, colour, or size). Check each thing matches the group before adding it.

rememberIt.hook: Before numbers: big/small, more/less, sort and match
rememberIt.unpack: Compare sizes, match one-to-one, sort by colour or shape. This builds 'how many' before counting.

studentQuestions.a: Comparing and sorting builds the sense of 'more' and 'less' - the ground counting stands on.
Pairing each item with one other (a cup for each saucer) - it shows equal, more, or fewer without counting.

video.veoPrompt:
Google Veo prompt pack — 6 clips x 5s each (30s total), with voice-over scripts. Generate each clip in order (Clip 1 first, then use Veo's "Extend" on each result for Clips 2-6) so Robo and the classroom stay consistent throughout:
  1. Paste "Clip 1" into veo.google or the Gemini app and generate it.
  2. On that result, tap "Extend" and paste "Clip 2" — do NOT start a new generation.
  3. Keep tapping "Extend" and pasting the next clip (3, 4, 5, then 6) in order.
  4. Clip 6 is what gives the video its goodbye/ending — don't stop before it.
Global rules baked into every clip below: Robo is the ONLY character and the only voice — one speaker, no narrator, no background music, no extra sound effects competing with the dialogue. Numbers in the voice-over are spelled out as words (e.g. "fifty", not "50") so they're read correctly; numbers shown on screen stay as short printed digits on simple props only — never as sentences or captions.

Each clip below has a PROMPT (what to paste as the visual direction) and a VOICE-OVER (the narration script to speak slowly and warmly, like reading to a young child).

Clip 1 (0-5s): The Welcome
Prompt: 3D Pixar-style animation. a friendly, cute robot named Robo stands in a bright, futuristic classroom with a large glowing screen behind it. Robo waves happily at the camera, big friendly eyes, warm expressive animation. Continuous smooth camera pan. No on-screen text anywhere.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "Hi friends! I'm Robo! Today we're going to learn about Getting Ready to Count — Big, Small, First, Last. Before numbers: big/small, more/less, sort and match" (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Clip 2 (5-10s): The First Idea
Prompt: Continuous shot in the same bright classroom. Robo points at the glowing screen, where a simple, easy-to-follow picture or diagram lights up in sync with what Robo is saying — one clear visual only, no sentences or words rendered on screen.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "Let's start simple. To compare SIZE: look at which takes more space — that is bigger." (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Clip 3 (10-15s): The Next Idea
Prompt: Continuous shot. Robo watches excitedly and gestures as the screen updates with a second, slightly bigger or contrasting picture that builds on the first one, still one clear visual at a time, no on-screen text.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "Now here's the next part. To find FIRST and LAST: look at the two ends of the line." (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Clip 4 (15-20s): Practice Time
Prompt: Continuous shot. Robo points at the glowing screen, where a single large, simple printed number (like a signboard or scoreboard digit — not a sentence) appears. Robo tilts its head as if thinking, then nods and smiles as a green checkmark and a little sparkle effect appear next to it.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "Let's try one together. Which is BIGGER: an elephant or a mouse? ... That's it — elephant!" (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Clip 5 (20-25s): One More Practice
Prompt: Continuous shot. A new single large printed number appears on the glowing screen the same way as before. Robo cheers and jumps slightly with excitement as the checkmark and sparkle effect appear.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "You're doing great! One more: Which is TALLER: a tree or a flower? ... Yes! tree! Well done!" (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Clip 6 (25-30s): The Goodbye
Prompt: Continuous shot in the same classroom, the glowing screen visible in the background. Robo turns back to face the camera, clapping its metal hands happily, and waves goodbye. Smooth fade out. No on-screen text.
Voice-over: Robo says (single speaker, warm and slow): "Great job today! Remember: Before numbers: compare SIZE (big/small, tall/short), find FIRST and LAST at the ends of a line, use POSITION words (on/under/inside), and SORT alike things together.. See you next time — bye bye!" (no subtitles, no on-screen captions of the spoken words)

Tips for the most accurate result (Veo is a generative model — no prompt guarantees a perfect take every single time):
  - Generate each clip 2-3 times and keep the best take; accuracy varies generation to generation.
  - If a word still comes out wrong, try spelling it phonetically in the Voice-over line and regenerate.
  - For lessons where every word must be exact, you can mute Veo's built-in audio on export and record your own narration over it instead — reading the Voice-over lines aloud, or using this app's own "Speak" voice.
